title: Tiered heartbeat orchestration and thresholded failover for SLO preservation
creator: Asha Patel
description:
Problem: We continue to see regional instability during partial infra degradation where simple readiness/liveness signals cause large autoscaler oscillations and aggressive failovers that violate our P95/P99 latency SLOs for latency-sensitive routes. Current single-threshold probes lead to cascading drain and recovery cycles that amplify tail latency and increase request errors during network blips and capacity pressure.

Goal: Implement a coordinated, tiered heartbeat orchestration and thresholded failover strategy that synthesizes multiple health signals into a graded readiness envelope per region, integrates with autoscaler damping, and applies tiered circuit-breaker actions (soft degrade -> partial admission -> hard reject) to keep critical SLOs intact.

Scope and approach:
- Build a lightweight "heartbeat-orchestrator" service that consumes existing health signals (probe latency, recent error rate, memory pressure, queue depth, KV cache hit ratio) and emits a single regional health envelope with numeric score and categorical tier (GREEN / YELLOW / ORANGE / RED).
- Define per-route contracts mapping to tiered actions: e.g., critical routes (tokenization/authorization) prefer conservative shedding; non-critical background rerankers can be shed early.
- Replace binary readiness gating with progressive thresholds and cooling windows. In YELLOW, start preferring local capacity and enable prefix caching; in ORANGE initiate soft-circuit limiting (slow-path tokens, smaller batch sizes) and begin admission control; in RED trigger regional failover and route to fallbacks or lower-cost model variants.
- Integrate the envelope into the autoscaler decision pipeline: autoscaler should respect graded health by increasing hysteresis and reducing scale-in aggressiveness for regions in YELLOW/ORANGE to avoid thrash.
- Implement synthetic warmup canaries: the rollout will use synthetic traffic with realistic request shapes to validate tier transitions and ensure stability before routing live traffic.

Metrics and SLOs to track:
- latency.p95 and latency.p99 per-route per-region (targets: p95 < 150ms for critical, p99 < 400ms)
- request_error_rate overall and per-tier (target < 0.5% for critical)
- autoscaler.scale_events per-hour and scale_in/scale_out ratio (goal: reduce unnecessary scale-ins by 50% during transient events)
- regional.failover_count and mean_time_to_recover (goal: fewer than 3 failovers per month per region)

Design trade-offs and rationale:
- Centralized vs decentralized orchestrator: a centralized orchestrator simplifies global policy and observability but is a single coordination point; therefore we will run a distributed, leader-elected orchestrator per-region that publishes its envelope to regional control-plane caching to avoid cross-region latency.
- Conservative shedding vs aggressive shedding: prioritizing SLOs for critical routes means accepting higher cost during degradation (short-term overprovision) rather than risking user-visible errors; we will offer opt-in aggressive shedding profiles for internal/experimental workloads.
- Tight coupling to autoscaler: we will expose the envelope through a stable contract (health_score + tier + last_transition_timestamp) and implement adapters on the autoscaler side to avoid coupling the orchestrator and autoscaler codebases.

Rollout plan:
- Phase 0 (staging): implement orchestrator and adapters; run in shadow mode consuming live signals but not affecting routing. Add dashboards: Grafana dashboard "Reliability / Heartbeat Orchestrator / Staging" (link in comments).
- Phase 1 (canary): enable synthesized traffic for one low-traffic region; validate tier transitions and autoscaler damping with real synthetic load.
- Phase 2 (selected routes): enable progressive gating on a small set of critical routes with longer cooling windows.
- Phase 3 (regional rollout): expand to all regions; monitor metrics and gradually shorten cooldown windows as confidence builds.

Testing and validation:
- Chaos tests: simulate network partition, delayed probe responses, and memory pressure to verify graceful degradation and no autoscaler thrash.
- Load tests: run mixed-workload replay to make sure batch adaptations and shedding policies maintain p95 targets.
- Eval hooks: add end-to-end synthetic canary checks and automated regression alerts tied to quality monitors (console alerts).

Runbook highlights:
- Automations: automated rollback if p99 latency or error rate exceed thresholds for more than 5 minutes during rollout.
- Manual steps: how to force a region to ORANGE/RED for emergency evacuation, and steps to drain with minimal user impact.

Open questions:
- Exact numeric mapping from health_score -> tier thresholds and cooling windows (proposal in Confluence).
- Per-customer overrides and how to reflect Dedicated/Private deployments where customer policies may differ.
- Billing implications of keeping higher capacity during YELLOW/ORANGE (prod finance review pending).

2026-03-11 - Design review with Reliability and Autoscaler teams. Agreed on per-region leader-elected orchestrator. Action: Asha to draft Confluence spec. Confluence draft: https://confluence.redwood.com/display/Reliability/Heartbeat+Orchestrator+Spec

2026-03-12 - Spike complete: small Node + Rust shim prototype that synthesizes health_score from probe latency and memory pressure. Spike repo: https://github.com/redwood/reliability-heartbeat-spike (PR #12)
2026-03-13 - Decision: autoscaler will use a 'health_holdoff' multiplier for scale-in decisions. Need autoscaler adapter (ENG-305111 dependency).

2026-03-14 - Implemented staging dashboard and synthetic canary harness. Grafana: https://grafana.redwood.com/d/Reliability/heartbeat-orchestrator-staging. Started shadow mode in us-east-1. Next: PR for orchestrator core (GH #3456).
